annotations.keyFindings: Emergency department visits over six months in 34 percent with weekly reporting against 41 percent with usual care; completion 83 percent in month one and 71 percent by month six.
annotations.limitations: Two centres with a dedicated alert nurse; older patients and those without home internet underrepresented.

annotations.keyFindings: In routine care for 1,480 patients, completion fell from 78 percent in month one to 46 percent by month six; lower at age 75 or over (odds ratio 0.52) and in the most deprived areas (odds ratio 0.61).
annotations.limitations: One centre; cannot separate improving symptoms from disengagement.

annotations.keyFindings: The 31 patients who stopped reporting cited unread answers, ill-fitting questions and device difficulty; several stopped after a severe report got no call within the day.
annotations.limitations: One urban centre; patients who needed an interpreter are missing.

annotations.keyFindings: Median 38 severe alerts a week; median time to nurse contact 3.1 hours on weekdays and 19.5 hours at weekends; 29 percent of alerts concerned known symptoms.
annotations.limitations: One unit; the weekend rota's effect was not measured.

annotations.keyFindings: Fourteen trials with 5,210 patients; emergency visits reduced in 6 of the 9 trials measuring them; quality of life favoured monitoring in 8 of 11.
annotations.limitations: Unblinded trials; adherence poorly reported; no outcomes for patients who stopped reporting.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 204 adults aged 75 and over, 57 percent chose paper; 18 percent of tablet users needed staff help.
annotations.limitations: Single visit; no follow-up of continued reporting.

annotations.keyFindings: Across three centres, completion fell most steeply after the first missed nurse response to a severe alert; centres with a same-day response standard recovered completion within three months.
annotations.limitations: Centres chose to take part; not designed to estimate effects on emergency visits.

claims.text: In a randomised trial of 612 adults starting chemotherapy, 34 percent with weekly reporting and 41 percent with usual care had at least one emergency department visit over six months.
claims.passage: Over six months, 34 percent of patients in the reporting group and 41 percent in the usual care group had at least one emergency department visit.
claims.interpretation: Weekly reporting can reduce emergency visits under trial conditions with a dedicated alert nurse.

claims.text: After routine rollout to 1,480 patients, completion of expected weekly reports fell from 78 percent in the first month to 46 percent by month six.
claims.passage: Completion of expected reports was 78 percent in the first month of treatment and 46 percent by month six.
claims.interpretation: In routine care the programme loses many patients by mid-treatment; completion is a measure that needs defining and tracking.

claims.interpretation: Weekend alert response must be measured separately.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Randomised trials and a review of 14 trials show that weekly electronic reporting can reduce emergency visits and protect quality of life under trial conditions with a dedicated alert nurse. In routine care, completion falls steeply by mid-treatment (78 to 46 percent in one centre), more among older and more deprived patients, and qualitative and mixed methods work links stopping to unanswered alerts, with weekend response particularly slow. Older adults often prefer paper. The effectiveness question has randomised answers; the unanswered question is how the programme is delivered and who it loses.
gradeRationale: Randomised trials and a review support a benefit on emergency visits (moderate certainty, lowered for lack of blinding and trial staffing); evidence on routine-care completion and its causes is observational and qualitative from single centres (low).
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty moderate for benefit, low for routine delivery.
